Tiny Earth catalase test procedure; adapted from Karen Reiner - Mircobe Library.  
  
 Hydrogen peroxide was added to smears of Ab+ isolates on microscope slides and observed for bubbles as an indicator of conversion of H2O2 to water and gaseous oxygen via catalase.

Protocol provided by Dr. González-Orta. 
  
 To test for Cytochrome C Oxidase, sterile toothpicks were used to place a colony of a target isolate onto filter paper with N,N-dimethyl-p-phenylenediamine in a petri plate. A pink product, indophenol, indicated metabolization of the artificial electron donor, N,N-dimethyl-p-phenylenediamine, via the electron transport chain using the carrier enzyme cytochrome C.

American Society for Microbiology's Blood Agar Plates and Hemolysis Protocol (Buxton 2005). 
  
 Using sterile toothpicks, isolates were streaked out onto blood agar plates and incubated at 28°C for 2 days. Interpretation of hemolysis on blood agar plates following beta, alpha and gamma hemolysis.

Tiny Earth Motility procedure; adapted from Gaston College - Gaston College.  
  
 Using sterile toothpicks, isolates were spot inoculated onto motility agar plates and incubated at 28°C for 2 days. Afterwards, plates were observed for movement from the initial inoculation spot.

American Society for Microbiology's Gelatin Hydrolysis Test Protocol (Dela Cruz and Torres 2012). 
  
 Test tubes filled prepared with nutrient gelatin were inoculated by stabbing a sterile needle with the target isolate. Tubes were then incubated at 28°C for 2 days; to confirm liquefaction due to gelatinase activity, tubes were immersed in ice for 15-30 minutes then removed and tilted to observe for hydrolysis even after the ice bath.

Adapted nitrate test protocol provided by Dr. González-Orta. 
  
 Test tubes with durham tubes filled with prepared nitrate were inoculated using a sterile loop to transfer a target isolate until turbid. Utilizing a modified procedure, 1-mL of liquid isolate culture was pipetted into a new 1.5-mL tube. Two drops of reagent A (sulfanilic acid) and reagent B (⍺-naphthylamine) are added. A change in color indicated nitrate reduction while gas in the original durham tube indicated denitrification.

American Society for Microbiology's Citrate Test Protocol (MacWilliams, 2009). 
  
 Using sterile toothpicks, isolates were transferred and spread towards the edges of the plate away from one another and incubated at 28°C for 2 days. Color change from green to an intense blue results from changes in pH as a by-product of citrate metabolism.

American Society for Microbiology's Starch Agar Protocol (Lal and Cheeptham 2021). 
  
 Using sterile toothpicks, isolates were spot inoculated onto starch agar plates and incubated at 28°C for 2 days. Afterwards, plates were flooded with iodine solution to record areas of yellowing and or zones of clearing, indicating starch hydrolysis.

American Society for Microbiology's Carbohydrate Fermentation Protocol (Reiner 2012). 
  
 Test tubes with durham tubes were filled with a prepared broth medium and inoculated with a target isolate colony using a sterile stick. Tubes were then incubated at 28°C for 2 days; changes in pH indicator, Bromocresol purple, from purple to yellow indicate acid products produced through fermentation. While bubbles within the durham tube indicated the production of gas.

 As a confirmatory test, using a sterile loop, smears of Ab+ isolates were made on slides and mixed with a few drops of 3% potassium hydroxide (KOH) to determine isolate cell wall structure.

1. Streak isolate on a blood agar plate. Incubate at 28C for 48h. 
 2. Observe isolate for alpha (partial), beta (complete), and gamma (no) hemolysis by noting color and size of zone of clearing.

1. Using a sterile stick, inoculate colony into gelatin-containing liquid media. Incubate at 28C for 48h. 
 2. Remove media tube from incubator and place on ice for 15 minutes.  
 3. Observe the presence of gelatinase by noting liquid (gelatinase +) or solid (gelatinase -) composition of the media after ice.

1. Spot-inoculate a colony onto motility agar using a sterile toothpick. Incubate at 28C for 48h. 
 2. Observe the presence of motility (colony expansion outward from spot) vs non-motility (colony size stays same).

1. Spot-inoculate a colony onto a starch agar plate using a sterile toothpick. Incubate at 28C for 48h. 
 2. Pour iodine over the plate post-incubation and observe for a zone of clearing around colonies (amylase positive) vs. no zone of clearing (amylase negative).

1. Swipe a colony across a Kovács oxidase reagent-soaked piece of filter paper using a sterile toothpick.  
 2. Observe purple color change after five minutes (cyt. c oxidase positive) vs. no color change (cyt. c oxidase negative).

1. Inoculate a colony into glucose and bromocresol purple-containing liquid media with an inverted Durham tube. Incubate at 28C for 48h. 
 2. Observe for glucose fermentation (yellow inside Durham tube) and gas production (bubble inside Durham tube) vs. no fermentation (tube remains purple) and no gas production (no bubble).

1. Streak a colony on a citrate agar plate containing bromothymol blue. Incubate at 28C for 48h. 
 2. Observe for blue color change (citrate permease positive) vs. no color change/stays green (citrate permease negative).

1. Inoculate a colony into a liquid culture containing nitrate broth and an inverted Durham tube. Incubate at 28C for 216 hours.  
 2. Check Durham tube for bubble formation (denitrification, N2 gas production) vs. no bubble (no denitrification, no N2 gas). 
 3. Aliquot 1000 uL of inoculated nitrate broth into an Eppendorf tube.  
 4. Add 2 drops of reagent A (sulfanilic acid), then 2 drops of reagent B (alpha-naphthylamine).  
 5. Observe for immediate red color change (nitrate reduction) vs. delayed or no color change (no nitrate reduction).

protocol:
Tiny Earth catalase test procedure; adapted from Karen Reiner - Mircobe Library.  
  
 Hydrogen peroxide was added to smears of Ab+ isolates on microscope slides and observed for bubbles as an indicator of conversion of H2O2 to water and gaseous oxygen via catalase.

Protocol provided by Dr. González-Orta. 
  
 To test for Cytochrome C Oxidase, sterile toothpicks were used to place a colony of a target isolate onto filter paper with N,N-dimethyl-p-phenylenediamine in a petri plate. A pink product, indophenol, indicated metabolization of the artificial electron donor, N,N-dimethyl-p-phenylenediamine, via the electron transport chain using the carrier enzyme cytochrome C.

American Society for Microbiology's Blood Agar Plates and Hemolysis Protocol (Buxton 2005). 
  
 Using sterile toothpicks, isolates were streaked out onto blood agar plates and incubated at 28°C for 2 days. Interpretation of hemolysis on blood agar plates following beta, alpha and gamma hemolysis.

Tiny Earth Motility procedure; adapted from Gaston College - Gaston College.  
  
 Using sterile toothpicks, isolates were spot inoculated onto motility agar plates and incubated at 28°C for 2 days. Afterwards, plates were observed for movement from the initial inoculation spot.

American Society for Microbiology's Gelatin Hydrolysis Test Protocol (Dela Cruz and Torres 2012). 
  
 Test tubes filled prepared with nutrient gelatin were inoculated by stabbing a sterile needle with the target isolate. Tubes were then incubated at 28°C for 2 days; to confirm liquefaction due to gelatinase activity, tubes were immersed in ice for 15-30 minutes then removed and tilted to observe for hydrolysis even after the ice bath.

Adapted nitrate test protocol provided by Dr. González-Orta. 
  
 Test tubes with durham tubes filled with prepared nitrate were inoculated using a sterile loop to transfer a target isolate until turbid. Utilizing a modified procedure, 1-mL of liquid isolate culture was pipetted into a new 1.5-mL tube. Two drops of reagent A (sulfanilic acid) and reagent B (⍺-naphthylamine) are added. A change in color indicated nitrate reduction while gas in the original durham tube indicated denitrification.

American Society for Microbiology's Citrate Test Protocol (MacWilliams, 2009). 
  
 Using sterile toothpicks, isolates were transferred and spread towards the edges of the plate away from one another and incubated at 28°C for 2 days. Color change from green to an intense blue results from changes in pH as a by-product of citrate metabolism.

American Society for Microbiology's Starch Agar Protocol (Lal and Cheeptham 2021). 
  
 Using sterile toothpicks, isolates were spot inoculated onto starch agar plates and incubated at 28°C for 2 days. Afterwards, plates were flooded with iodine solution to record areas of yellowing and or zones of clearing, indicating starch hydrolysis.

American Society for Microbiology's Carbohydrate Fermentation Protocol (Reiner 2012). 
  
 Test tubes with durham tubes were filled with a prepared broth medium and inoculated with a target isolate colony using a sterile stick. Tubes were then incubated at 28°C for 2 days; changes in pH indicator, Bromocresol purple, from purple to yellow indicate acid products produced through fermentation. While bubbles within the durham tube indicated the production of gas.

Protocol provided by Dr. González-Orta. 
  
 As a confirmatory test, using a sterile loop, smears of Ab+ isolates were made on slides and mixed with a few drops of 3% potassium hydroxide (KOH) to determine isolate cell wall structure.

Protocol: 
 Inoculate a tube of SIM media using an inoculating wire or needle. Pick a bacterial colony with a sterile inoculating wire and stab straight down through the agar towards the bottom of the tube and quickly withdraw the wire along the same path. Do not move the wire around in the agar. 
 Sterilize the wire with a flame after each inoculation. 
 For control, repeat steps 1-2 with sterile needle 
 Incubate the tubes at the optimal growth temperature (25ºC) for 5 days. 
 Examine the tubes for evidence of hydrogen sulfide production (browning or blackening of the media). Record the results. 
 Examine the tubes for evidence of motility, cloudiness or turbidity of the media that extends outside of the stab line into the surrounding agar. Nonmotile bacteria will only exhibit growth in the stab line.  
 After recording your sulfide and motility results, test for indole by adding 1-2 ml of Kovac’s reagent to the SIM tube. Indole is present if a cherry red color develops on the surface of the culture medium. 
 Record your data in the chart. Include a photo of your SIM tubes.

1. Inoculate a colony into a liquid culture containing nitrate broth and an inverted Durham tube. Incubate at 28C for 216 hours.

 3. Aliquot 1000 uL of inoculated nitrate broth into an Eppendorf tube.  
 4. Add 2 drops of reagent A (sulfanilic acid), then 2 drops of reagent B (alpha-naphthylamine).  
 5. Observe for immediate red color change (nitrate reduction) vs. delayed or no color change (no nitrate reduction).

1. Obtain enough blood agar plates for my samples and divide the plates into two sections so one bacteria is on one side and another is on the other side. 
 2. Label the bottom of the plates (both sides) with initials, date, and bacteria/number. (One bacteria will be on one side and a different one on the other side, so label them separately.) 
 3. Use a sterile toothpick to touch a bacterial colony to transfer it to the plate. 
 4. Streak the sample into the corresponding section by moving the toothpick back and forth (like tri-streaking, just only the first streak.) Make sure to keep the samples in their designated area and don't get too close to the other section to avoid cross-contamination. 
 5. Repeat these steps for the other plates and bacteria samples. Be sure to use a new toothpick every time. 
 6. Store your plates agar side up and leave them to inoculate until next class.

1. Label test tubes containing agar medium with initials, date, sample to be tested, and agar type. (motility test medium, motility - indole - lysine) 
 2. Using the stick with the thin, long metal on the end, heat it over the Bunsen burner until it turns orange, so that it cleans it and kills any bacteria on it.  
 3. Let it cool and then pick up a single colony from the sample being used. Stick the end of the metal about halfway down into the semi-solid agar medium.  
 4. Pull it straight out of the medium to keep the same line as it entered the medium. 
 5. Incubate/grow the test tubes at 35 degrees C for 18 hours until growth is evident. Can incubate for up to 7 days. Repeat these steps for all bacteria samples.  
 6. Observe the test tubes carefully and look for signs of growth.  
 7. Be sure to let the metal cool before collecting a bacteria sample so it doesn't kill the bacteria. 
 8. Be sure to heat the metal between every use of a different bacteria sample.
